1Introduction

1.1  Main Focus and Dataset

The exercise aims to find the effect of personal characteristics on wages. I sequentially use four panel data methods — Pooled OLS, First Difference, Fixed Effects and Random Effects — and find a proper model for this problem by comparing the efficiency of the four methods. The panel dataset nlswork.dta is used in the exercise. It contains wage variables in logarithmic form and other personal characteristics like age, experience, etc. The key variables are:

VariableDescriptionRole
ln_wageIndividual log wage from 1968 to 1988 (except 1974, 1976, 1979, 1981, 1984, 1986); constrained to wages above $1/hour and below $700/hourDependent
ageCurrent ageExplanatory
ttl_expCurrent years of total work experienceExplanatory
tenureCurrent years of tenure on the current jobExplanatory
raceWhether black (White / Black / Other, entered as dummies)Explanatory
not_smsaWhether residing in an area not designated a standard metropolitan statistical areaExplanatory
southWhether residing in the SouthExplanatory
The dataset has 18 key independent variables but I only use 6 of them. I do not select grade (completed years of schooling) because in the panel dataframe it equals 12 for everyone — education level has no variation, so studying its effect on wages is meaningless, and it would cause a Singular matrix error in the first-difference estimation.

1.2  Econometric Methods

Since four different methods are used, I explain each model in detail. (Note: to simplify the time index, t runs from 1 to T representing 1968, 1969, …, 1988; the same labeling applies to individual i.)

Method 1 Pooled OLS

We assume the effect is the same for all individuals and time points — there is no unobservable individual-specific effect αi in the model:

  • xit = (xit1, …, xitk)′ is a k-dimensional vector of regressors for individual i at time t, not including a constant;
  • yi = (yi1, …, yiT)′ stacks the dependent observations of individual i;
  • εi = (εi1, …, εiT)′ is the error term.

Method 2 First Difference

First differencing is another way to eliminate the individual effects, using differences in y:

where Δyit = yit − yi,t−1, ΔXit′ = Xit′ − Xi,t−1′ and Δεit = εit − εi,t−1.

We used the fact that Δαit = αi − αi = 0.

Method 3 Fixed Effects

Fixed effects models control for individual-specific unobservable heterogeneity by introducing individual fixed effects αi:

To estimate the fixed effects model, we subtract the time-averaged values for each individual:

By removing the fixed characteristics of an individual, we can control for factors that do not vary with time. We can then apply pooled OLS on this “time-demeaned” equation to estimate β.

Method 4 Random Effects

For the random effect model we assume the individual effect ui is random and uncorrelated with the explanatory variables, Cov(ui | Xit) = 0. The model is:

where Xit′β = β1Xit1 + ⋯ + βkXitk and the δt represent different time intercepts. Define the parameter

RE can then be considered a partially time-demeaned equation:

By now, we can apply pooled OLS estimation on this equation.

1.3  Challenges in Python Programming

  • Perfect collinearity. It is common when estimating panel data and prevents using a single model to estimate the effects of all variables. I use linearmodels.panel to estimate all models, which may cause bias. For a more general condition I also code manually with NumPy, which helps me recognize the bias and obtain more precise results.
  • Matrix size & memory. The biggest problem when coding manually with NumPy is that the dataframe is very large, making matrix operations slow or impossible. I considered scipy.sparse, but after rechecking the data I found that only the correct number of individuals is needed to compute manually — the matrix can then be calculated correctly (discussed in §4.2 Fixed Effects).
  • Python–Stata integration. Stata has an advantage in the reliability and stability of results for complex statistical analyses, so the final conclusions are given by the results from Stata.

2Data Cleaning

Before data analysis, the first thing is to import and clean the data. The data is stored as .dta in Stata format.

import pandas as pd

# Loading data
data = pd.read_stata("nlswork.dta")

# Create dummies
data['white'] = (data['race'] == 'White').astype(int)
data['black'] = (data['race'] == 'Black').astype(int)
data['other'] = (data['race'] == 'Other').astype(int)

# Drop missing values
data_cleaned = data.dropna()
data_cleaned.head(len(data_cleaned))

drop if missing_flag > 0
drop missing_flag
sum ln_wage age ttl_exp tenure race11 race12 race13 not_smsa south
''')

4Econometric Analysis

Now let’s do the particular econometric analysis for the question mentioned in the introduction. The frame of this section is divided into three parts:

  1. Estimation with linearmodels.panel. This subsection uses the estimation functions in the linearmodels package for the four models. The advantage is the simplicity of the estimated models and the very easy, readable code implementation. However, different models may have different restrictions on the data, and the conditions under which the models apply need to be considered. This solution is more efficient than coding in NumPy since it achieves the estimation with fewer lines.
  2. Coding in NumPy. This subsection estimates the models with NumPy, which requires a manual implementation of the estimation process — constructing the estimating function, calculating standard errors, etc. It demands a clear understanding of the structure of the panel data (both the individual and time dimensions) to ensure proper processing of the data and estimation of the model.
  3. Testing. This subsection uses tests to compare the efficiency of each model. Since the linearmodels package is more efficient than the NumPy method, I focus on the first subsection.

4.1  Estimation with linearmodels.panel

This section mainly uses linearmodels.panel to do the estimation. First install the module:

pip install linearmodels

This module contains five kinds of estimations for different models. In this exercise I only use four functions from linearmodels.panel:

from linearmodels import PooledOLS
from linearmodels import FirstDifferenceOLS
from linearmodels import PanelOLS
from linearmodels import RandomEffects

1. Pooled OLS

The model is given in the “Econometric Methods” part. To make it more readable, I simplify it as:

I use PooledOLS from linearmodels to estimate the coefficient of each variable. Note: race contains three dummies, and we cannot include all of them in the model because of perfect collinearity.

import statsmodels.api as sm

# Setting the indices of i and t
data_P = data_cleaned.set_index(['idcode', 'year'])
# Define the dependent and independent variables
y = data_P['ln_wage']
X = data_P[['age', 'ttl_exp', 'tenure', 'white', 'black', 'not_smsa', 'south']]
# Add constant
X = sm.add_constant(X)
# Estimate the model
model = PooledOLS(y, X)
results_OLS = model.fit()
# Print the output
print(results_OLS.summary)

2. First Difference

Similar to the PooledOLS estimation, there is no individual fixed effect in the model. Before doing the FD estimation, we have to preprocess the data with a first-order difference:

# Create first differences for variables
data_FD = data_cleaned.sort_values(by=['idcode', 'year'])
data_FD['d_ln_wage'] = data_FD.groupby('idcode')['ln_wage'].diff()
data_FD['d_age']     = data_FD.groupby('idcode')['age'].diff()
data_FD['d_ttl_exp'] = data_FD.groupby('idcode')['ttl_exp'].diff()
data_FD['d_tenure']  = data_FD.groupby('idcode')['tenure'].diff()
data_FD

data_FD.head() — first differences by individual (idcode 1 and 5159 shown; [13452 rows × 28 columns])
I did not include the variables race, not_smsa and south above: individual fixed effects are eliminated by calculating the difference between the same subject at different points in time, whereas these three variables do not change over shorter periods (race does not change over time, and changes of residence are infrequent), so first-order differencing them is inappropriate or meaningless. Also, the same value of a variable at different times leads to a missing value after differencing. I clean data_FD and drop the missing values to avoid errors.
# Drop the missing values
data_FD = data_FD.dropna(subset=['d_ln_wage', 'd_age', 'd_ttl_exp', 'd_tenure'])
# Setting the indices of i and t
data_FD.set_index(['idcode', 'year'], inplace=True)
# Define the dependent and independent variables
y_diff = data_FD['d_ln_wage']
X_diff = data_FD[['d_age', 'd_ttl_exp', 'd_tenure']]
# Estimate the model
model = FirstDifferenceOLS(y_diff, X_diff)
results_FD = model.fit()
# Print the output
print(results_FD.summary)

Hence, I next run the fixed effect model and random effect model to demonstrate it.

Collinearity check for the FD model

First difference is the most likely to cause collinearity. I check the correlation and variance inflation factors (VIF) to examine the collinearity in the first-difference model:

3. Fixed Effects

Now consider the individual fixed effects αi. As mentioned in the Econometric Methods part, the operation of “time-demeaning” is necessary for the estimation. In Python we don’t need to do this manually, because PanelOLS from linearmodels.panel will do it automatically.

# Setting the indices of i and t
data_FE = data_cleaned.set_index(['idcode', 'year'])
# Define the dependent and independent variables
y = data_FE['ln_wage']
X = data_FE[['age', 'ttl_exp', 'tenure', 'white', 'black', 'not_smsa', 'south']]
X = sm.add_constant(X)
# Estimate the model
model = PanelOLS(y, X, entity_effects=True, drop_absorbed=True)
results_FE = model.fit()
# Print the output
print(results_FE.summary)

From the result table above, the program automatically removes the time-invariant variables white and black to ensure non-perfect collinearity. In the fixed effects model these variables are fully absorbed (fully covariate with other variables), making it impossible to estimate their effects on ln_wage separately — the fixed effects absorb all time-invariant individual characteristics.

The results show a negative impact of age, not_smsa and south, and a positive impact of ttl_exp and tenure, on wage.

4. Random Effects

So what do we know about the effect of white and black? The answer is the Random Effects model. The random effects model assumes that individual effects are random and includes these time-invariant characteristics, so that the coefficients on these variables can be estimated. The assumptions are

Then the model can be estimated correctly. (Note: race contains three dummies and we cannot include all of them because of perfect collinearity.)

from linearmodels.panel import RandomEffects

# Setting the indices of i and t
data_RE = data_cleaned.set_index(['idcode', 'year'])
# Define the dependent and independent variables
y = data_RE['ln_wage']
X = data_RE[['age', 'ttl_exp', 'tenure', 'white', 'black', 'not_smsa', 'south']]
X = sm.add_constant(X)
# Estimate the model
model = RandomEffects(y, X)
results_RE = model.fit()
# Print the output
print(results_RE.summary)

The result is similar to the fixed effect model, and the random effect results show a negative impact of race on wage. What I concentrate on most is the R-squared value: the R² of the fixed effect model is 0.1315 while that of the random effect model is 0.3605. These values suggest the two models may not fit well, reflecting that we may need to do some tests to find which model is the most efficient. The test is discussed in subsection 4.3.

4.2  Coding in NumPy

In this section I use the NumPy method to estimate the four models. I calculate the standard error, z-statistic and confidence interval for further explanation of the fitness of each model. The method is:

The OLS coefficient:

To calculate the standard error, first calculate the residuals:

Since σ² is unknown, we replace it with a consistent estimator:

Then write down the variance–covariance matrix:

Var(β0)Cov(β0, β1)Cov(β0, β2)⋯Cov(β0, βk)
Cov(β1, β0)Var(β1)Cov(β1, β2)⋯Cov(β1, βk)
Cov(β2, β0)Cov(β2, β1)Var(β2)⋯Cov(β2, βk)
⋮⋮⋮⋱⋮
Cov(βk, β0)Cov(βk, β1)Cov(βk, β2)⋯Var(βk)

The standard error is then obtained from the square root of the diagonal of this matrix. Notes: in calculating σ², the denominator is the degrees of freedom of the residual e in the model; to avoid perfect collinearity, other is excluded from the model.

Similar to the last subsection, I import NumPy for coding convenience. Coding manually, identifying n, T and k is vitally important — especially in the Fixed Effects and Random Effects models, where memory constraints can prevent computers from calculating matrices with numerous values and may cause the @ operation to fail. In the dataframe I used, after data cleaning there are 13,452 rows in total containing T = 12 time observations for each individual, so I calculate n = 13452 / T = 1121; k is the number of independent variables, set as k = np.shape(X)[1].

from scipy import stats
import numpy as np

n = 1121   # Number of individuals
T = 12     # Time periods

1. Pooled OLS

data_cleaned.set_index(['idcode', 'year'], inplace=True)
# Transform the DataFrame to numpy arrays
X = data_cleaned[['age', 'ttl_exp', 'tenure', 'white', 'black', 'not_smsa', 'south']].to_numpy()
y = data_cleaned['ln_wage'].to_numpy()
k = np.shape(X)[1]
# Add constant
X = np.column_stack((np.ones(len(y)), X))
# Estimate beta
beta_hat = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T @ y
# Standard error
e = y - X @ beta_hat
sigma2 = np.sum(e ** 2) / (n - k)
var_cov_matrix = sigma2 * np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)
se = np.sqrt(np.diag(var_cov_matrix))
# z-statistic
t_stats = beta_hat / se
# Set the confidence level (alpha) as 5%
alpha = 0.05
critical_value = np.abs(stats.t.ppf(alpha / 2, df=k))
# Confidence interval
conf_int = np.column_stack((beta_hat - critical_value * se,
                            beta_hat + critical_value * se))
# Tabulate the results
results = pd.DataFrame({"Coefficient": beta_hat, "Standard Error": se,
                        "t-statistic": t_stats,
                        "95% CI Lower": conf_int[:, 0], "95% CI Upper": conf_int[:, 1]})
print(results)

# Setting the indices of i and t
data_cleaned.set_index(['idcode', 'year'], inplace=True)

X = data_cleaned[['age', 'ttl_exp', 'tenure']].to_numpy()

y_diff = y[1:] - y[:-1]
X_diff = X[1:] - X[:-1]
# Drop missing values
missing_indices = np.any(np.isnan(X_diff), axis=1)
X_diff = X_diff[~missing_indices]
y_diff = y_diff[~missing_indices]
k = X_diff.shape[1]
# beta_hat
beta_hat_diff = np.linalg.inv(X_diff.T @ X_diff) @ X_diff.T @ y_diff
# Standard error
e_diff = y_diff - X_diff @ beta_hat_diff
sigma2_diff = np.sum(e_diff ** 2) / (n - k)
var_cov_matrix_diff = sigma2_diff * np.linalg.inv(X_diff.T @ X_diff)
se_diff = np.sqrt(np.diag(var_cov_matrix_diff))
# z-statistic
t_stats_diff = beta_hat_diff / se_diff
# Confidence level (alpha) 5%
alpha = 0.05
critical_value_diff = np.abs(stats.t.ppf(alpha / 2, df=k))
conf_int_diff = np.column_stack((beta_hat_diff - critical_value_diff * se_diff,
                                 beta_hat_diff + critical_value_diff * se_diff))
results_diff = pd.DataFrame({"Coefficient": beta_hat_diff, "Standard Error": se_diff,
                             "t-statistic": t_stats_diff,
                             "95% CI Lower": conf_int_diff[:, 0],
                             "95% CI Upper": conf_int_diff[:, 1]})
print(results_diff)

3. Fixed Effects

The linear regression model is y = Dα + Xβ + ε. We would like to estimate only β by using the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell (FWL) theorem. The core idea of this approach is to define a projection matrix P and the corresponding orthogonal projection matrix Q:

Then Qy is the residual in the regression of y on Q, and QX refers to the residuals in the regression of X on Q. The OLS estimate of β by the FWL theorem is

For simplicity, I express Q = InT − In ⊗ (ιTιT′ / T):

By the standard OLS estimator, the BLUE estimator of β is

where

After these operations, I conduct the method in this subsection to estimate the fixed effects estimators.

# Setting the indices of i and t
data_cleaned.set_index(['idcode', 'year'], inplace=True)
# Transform dataframe to numpy arrays
y = data_cleaned['ln_wage'].to_numpy()
X = data_cleaned[['age', 'ttl_exp', 'tenure', 'not_smsa', 'south']].to_numpy()
k = np.shape(X)[1]
# Get Q matrix
Q = np.eye(n*T) - np.kron(np.eye(n), 1/T*np.ones((T, T)))
Q = np.eye(n*T) - np.kron(np.eye(n), 1/T*np.ones((T, T)))
# Estimate beta
beta_hat_FE = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ Q @ X) @ X.T @ (Q @ y)
# Standard error
e_FE = Q @ y - (Q @ X) @ beta_hat_FE
sigma2_FE = np.sum(e_FE ** 2) / (n*T - n - k)
var_cov_matrix_FE = sigma2_FE * np.linalg.inv(X.T @ Q @ X)
se_FE = np.sqrt(np.diag(var_cov_matrix_FE))
# z-statistics
t_stats_FE = beta_hat_FE / se_FE
# Confidence level (alpha) 5%
alpha = 0.05
critical_value_FE = np.abs(stats.t.ppf(alpha / 2, df=k))
conf_int_FE = np.column_stack((beta_hat_FE - critical_value_FE * se_FE,
                               beta_hat_FE + critical_value_FE * se_FE))
results_FE = pd.DataFrame({"Coefficient": beta_hat_FE, "Standard Error": se_FE,
                           "t-statistic": t_stats_FE,
                           "95% CI Lower": conf_int_FE[:, 0],
                           "95% CI Upper": conf_int_FE[:, 1]})
print(results_FE)

4. Random Effects

Generalized Least Squares (GLS) estimator:

where Ω contains unknown quantities of σ2ε and σ2α and should be consistently estimated in advance. In detail,

where

Thus we obtain

Therefore

with a consistent variance estimator

# Setting the indices of i and t
data_cleaned.set_index(['idcode', 'year'], inplace=True)
# Transform the dataframe to numpy arrays
y = data_cleaned['ln_wage'].to_numpy()
X = data_cleaned[['age', 'ttl_exp', 'tenure', 'not_smsa', 'south']].to_numpy()
# Get Q matrix
Q = np.eye(n * T) - np.kron(np.eye(n), 1 / T * np.ones((T, T)))
# Between estimator
P = np.eye(n * T) - Q
beta_b = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ P @ X) @ X.T @ P @ y
# Within estimator
beta_w = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ Q @ X) @ X.T @ Q @ y
# Calculate RSS_b and RSS_w
PyPxb = P @ y - P @ X @ beta_b
QyQxb = Q @ y - Q @ X @ beta_w
RSS_b = PyPxb.T @ PyPxb
RSS_w = QyQxb.T @ QyQxb
# Degrees of freedom and error variances
k = X.shape[1]
sigma2_e = 1 / (n * T - n - k) * RSS_w
sigma2_a = 1 / (n * T - k * T - T) * RSS_b
# Omega matrix
omega = sigma2_e * np.eye(n * T) + sigma2_a * np.kron(np.eye(n), np.ones((T, T)))
# FGLS estimator
inv_omega = np.linalg.inv(omega)
beta_fgls = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ inv_omega @ X) @ X.T @ inv_omega @ y
var_fgls = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ inv_omega @ X)
# Standard errors
se_fgls = np.sqrt(np.diag(var_fgls))
# z-statistic
z_stats_fgls = beta_fgls / se_fgls
# Confidence level 0.05
alpha = 0.05
critical_value_fgls = np.abs(stats.norm.ppf(alpha / 2))
conf_int_fgls = np.column_stack((beta_fgls - critical_value_fgls * se_fgls,
                                 beta_fgls + critical_value_fgls * se_fgls))
results_fgls = pd.DataFrame({"Coefficient": beta_fgls, "Standard Error": se_fgls,
                             "z-statistic": z_stats_fgls,
                             "95% CI Lower": conf_int_fgls[:, 0],
                             "95% CI Upper": conf_int_fgls[:, 1]})
print(results_fgls)

Similar to the Fixed Effects model, I use the partial time-demean method to estimate the Random Effects model. (Note: I consulted ChatGPT for this partial time-demean method, and this code was generated by AI.)
# Setting the indices of i and t
data_cleaned.set_index(['idcode', 'year'], inplace=True)
# Define independent and dependent variables
y = data_cleaned['ln_wage']
X = data_cleaned[['age', 'ttl_exp', 'tenure', 'not_smsa', 'south']]

# Generated by AI — averages
y_mean = y.groupby(level='idcode').transform('mean')
X_mean = X.groupby(level='idcode').transform('mean')
# Calculate error variances
e_it = y - y_mean
sigma2_e = np.var(e_it)
sigma2_a = np.var(y_mean - np.mean(y_mean))
# theta
theta = 1 - np.sqrt(1 / (1 + T * (sigma2_a / sigma2_e)))
# Partial time demean
y_part_demeaned = y - theta * y_mean
X_part_demeaned = X - theta * X_mean
# Transform to numpy
y_part_demeaned = y_part_demeaned.to_numpy()
X_part_demeaned = X_part_demeaned.to_numpy()
k = X_part_demeaned.shape[1]
# Estimate beta
beta_hat_RE = np.linalg.inv(X_part_demeaned.T @ X_part_demeaned) @ X_part_demeaned.T @ y_part_demeaned
# Standard error
e_RE = y_part_demeaned - X_part_demeaned @ beta_hat_RE
sigma2_u = np.sum(e_RE ** 2) / (n * T - n - k)
var_cov_matrix_RE = sigma2_u * np.linalg.inv(X_part_demeaned.T @ X_part_demeaned)
se_RE = np.sqrt(np.diag(var_cov_matrix_RE))
# z-statistics
z_stats_RE = beta_hat_RE / se_RE
alpha = 0.05
critical_value_RE = np.abs(stats.norm.ppf(alpha / 2))
conf_int_RE = np.column_stack((beta_hat_RE - critical_value_RE * se_RE,
                               beta_hat_RE + critical_value_RE * se_RE))
results_RE = pd.DataFrame({"Coefficient": beta_hat_RE, "Standard Error": se_RE,
                           "z-statistic": z_stats_RE,
                           "95% CI Lower": conf_int_RE[:, 0],
                           "95% CI Upper": conf_int_RE[:, 1]})
print(results_RE)

4.3  Hausman Test

Now let’s come back to the question in subsection 4.1: how do we choose between the FE and RE models? If the individual units can be regarded as homogeneous, then it is reasonable to use the RE model. If the additional assumption for RE is too strong to hold in reality, it is always better to use FE. The Hausman test (Hausman, 1978; Hausman and Taylor, 1981) helps us make this choice. The typical version of the Hausman test is to check

Rewrite the hypotheses:

H0: Both FE and RE are consistent but RE is more efficient.

H1: FE is consistent but RE is not.

Therefore, if we reject the null, then FE is reasonable. The test statistic can be formulated as

Under the null, H ∼ χ²(k), where k is the number of regressors in the within regression (the number of time-variant variables used in the FE model). We need to check that the variance–covariance matrix Var(β̂W) − Var(β̂FGLS) is positive definite. If it is positive definite, follow the standard Hausman test above. If not, conduct the robust Hausman test, whose statistic is

Here the variance–covariance matrix is positive definite only under the robust version, and we can compare the statistic with the χ² critical value.

from scipy.stats import chi2

diff_beta = beta_hat_FE - beta_fgls
diff_var = var_cov_matrix_FE - var_fgls

if np.all(np.linalg.eigvals(diff_var) > 0):
    hausman_stat = np.dot(np.dot(diff_beta.T, np.linalg.inv(diff_var)), diff_beta)
    # print the test output
    print('Hausman Test Statistic:', hausman_stat)
    print('Degrees of Freedom:', df)
    print('Hausman Test p-value:', chi2.ppf(1 - .05, df=k))
    # Decide whether to reject the null
    if hausman_stat > chi2.ppf(1 - .05, df=k):
        print("Reject the null hypothesis: Fixed Effects model is preferred.")
    else:
        print("Fail to reject the null hypothesis: Random Effects model is preferred.")
else:
    print("The difference of variance matrix is not positive definite of standard Hausman test.")
    print("Use robust Hausman test.")
    robust_var_diff = var_cov_matrix_FE + var_fgls
    print("The difference of variance matrix is positive definite:",
          np.all(np.linalg.eigvals(robust_var_diff) > 0))
    hausman_stat = np.dot(np.dot(diff_beta.T, np.linalg.inv(robust_var_diff)), diff_beta)
    # print the test output
    print('Hausman Test Statistic:', hausman_stat)
    print('Degrees of Freedom:', df)
    print('Hausman Test p-value:', chi2.ppf(1 - .05, df=k))
    # Decide whether to reject the null
    if hausman_stat > chi2.ppf(1 - .05, df=k):
        print("Reject the null hypothesis: Fixed Effects model is preferred.")
    else:
        print("Fail to reject the null hypothesis: Random Effects model is preferred.")
The difference of variance matrix is not positive definite of standard Hausman test.
Use robust Hausman test.
The difference of variance matrix is positive definite: True
Hausman Test Statistic: 4571.8444285992155
Degrees of Freedom: 5
Hausman Test p-value: 11.070497693516351
Reject the null hypothesis: Fixed Effects model is preferred.

✅ Hausman test result

The standard Hausman variance difference is not positive definite, so the robust version is used. The robust statistic H = 4571.84 far exceeds the χ²(5) critical value of 11.07 at the 5% level, so we reject H0 — the Fixed Effects model is preferred.

🔎 What the Stata cross-check shows

I find that the race variables are most likely to induce endogeneity, and the variables which cause collinearity are all omitted in the Stata method. These results show that my model choices in Python were exactly correct. Then comes the conclusion.

5Conclusion

5.1  Empirical Analysis

By now, I have finished all the analysis. I summarize the impact effects below:

  1. age (current age): In all models the coefficients are negative but close to zero, and the t-statistics show a significant result.
  2. ttl_exp (current years worked): The coefficients are positive, a little far away from zero, and the t-statistics show a significant result.
  3. tenure (current years of tenure on the current job): The coefficient is positive and the t-statistic shows a significant result.
  4. race (black, white, other): The impact effect of this variable is the most complicated. The coefficients are negative if the race is black or white, and the t-statistic shows a not-that-significant result.
  5. not_smsa (live in a metropolitan area or not): The coefficient is negative and the impact effect is really large; the t-statistic shows a significant result.
  6. south (live in the South or not): The coefficient is negative and the impact effect is large; the t-statistic shows a significant result.

I conclude that although age has a negative effect on wages, this effect is small and close to zero, suggesting that age is not a major factor in wages. Current years worked and current years of tenure on the current job can be summarized as experience — whether in education or on the job. These two variables show a similar effect on wage: more experience leads to a higher wage. Employees’ race has little effect on their wage: the small t-statistic shows this effect is not significantly different from zero, so I conclude race does not affect individuals’ rewards on the job — but this is only in the white population. Being black reduces the wage more than being white, reflecting that there is racial discrimination in the workplace. Finally, not_smsa and south describe the living place of the workers: whether the residential address is an urban area and whether it is in the southern United States both matter for wages. Those who live outside the city limits and those who live in the North have lower wages than those who live in the city and in the South.

  • I first begin with the pooled OLS model, whose assumption is that all intercept terms are identical and that differences between individuals are not taken into account. This is obviously false, because race can be seen as an individual fixed effect — ignoring it makes a large bias.
  • After that, knowing the individual effect cannot be neglected, I use first difference to eliminate this effect. After differencing, the individual fixed effects are successfully eliminated, but the R² is almost zero, representing that the FD model does not fit well.
  • The fixed effects model assumes that individual effects are constant and correlated with the explanatory variables — each individual has its own unique intercept. The random effects model assumes random individual effects. These two models fit well, and I did the Hausman test to check which is more efficient. The answer is the Fixed Effects model.

5.2  Problem Unaddressed

race contains three kinds of races: white, black, other. Since including all these variables in a linear model causes endogeneity, only white and black can be included in the model. How can I solve this endogeneity problem? I believe that instrumental variables is the best way. Because of the space of the exercise and data limitations, I was unable to set up instrumental variables to solve the endogeneity problem of the original regression model in this panel-data analysis.
